Spending data and its patterns are synth: Spending data and its patterns are synthetic. Player metrics come from real Riot API snapshots. This small example shows how a private purchase endpoint could join an existing analytical pipeline.
League of Legends is a competitive game: League of Legends is a competitive game where players choose characters called **champions**. **Tier** describes competitive rank; **mastery** records experience with those characters. The real project studies character specialization and rank progression. This opening sample adds fictional purchases to demonstrate a familiar business reporting use case.
I’m a software developer moving from mob:
I’m a software developer moving from mobile games into data engineering. I built this project to practice reliable API collection, historical warehouse modeling and a usable analytical product. The real Riot API branch handles rate limits, retries, player refresh and rank/mastery snapshots. dbt turns those snapshots into player profiles and rank-period analysis.

The separate business branch freezes a ranked-player cohort, generates historical transactions and builds one spending mart. Anonymous Parquet exports serve this dashboard without exposing player IDs or warehouse credentials. [Source code and modeling documentation](https://github.com/Pedro-Iaki/league-specialization-etl)
**Role** approximates a player's usual p: **Role** approximates a player's usual position in the game. **Primary champion** is the leading character in their recent pool. **Playstyle** describes that pool's concentration, from specialists focused on a few characters to generalists using a wider mix. A higher **leading-champion share** indicates concentration; higher **normalized entropy** indicates more even use across the pool. These are inferred profile traits.
